title: Constantly reshape the world beneath your feet in the reality-bending "puzzle-first" Uncanyon, the next game from the devs behind the trippy Maquette
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
You think there's a Grand Uncanyon in this thing?

A problem that games have, I find, is that it's quite hard for them to inspire a sense of wonder. The kind of thing that old movies, before CGI, that would make you think, "how did they do that?" But games are all CGI, spiritually anyway, so it's a bit harder for the craft itself to truly wow in terms of not being able to comprehend how something works. However! I felt that today when I saw the reveal trailer for Uncanyon, a puzzle game from the devs behind Maquette set in the seam between unparallel realities where the very shape of the world is constantly in flux.

In Uncanyon, which also happens to be the name of the setting of the game, you play as Sonia, a "young woman who tumbles into this new and fantastical world, where hills breathe, trees change color, and the land itself never stands still," as the game's Steam page explains. It's that last part about the land never staying still that gave me pause when watching the reveal trailer, that wanted me to ask how it was made. The puzzles, in part, appear to involve changing the very shape of the world, parts of it morphing from one vibe to another almost seamlessly.

It's this transition that befuddled me, in the way you get confused for a while when watching someone cutting up a chocolate bar and convincing you there's suddenly more of it. It's delightful! I'm sure there's a real, technical explanation to all of it, the surreality of it all just caught me off guard in a way I've been craving for a while. How the puzzles themselves work isn't entirely clear, it was a short trailer, but from what I gather it involves things like timing the movement of rolling barrels just right to shape the land to your advantage.

A tidbit of combat could be seen too, which is less interesting to me. Uncanyon is described as "puzzle-first," so I suppose that means action-second. Hopefully we won't have to do all that much of that, I'd rather just see the ways the world twists and contorts in reaction to my puzzle solving. There's no exact release date attached to Uncanyon just yet, but it is due out sometime in 2027. You can wishlist it on Steam here.

title: Blizzard just announced Diablo 5, and this time the heroes have already lost
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Talk of the devil.

Blizzard has officially announced Diablo 5, confirming the next mainline entry in the series is expected to arrive in spring 2029.

Announced during BlizzCon 2026's opening ceremony, Blizzard has flipped the franchise's usual setup, as every prior Diablo game has centred on stopping an apocalypse before it happens, and this one starts after one is already underway.

According to Blizzard, Diablo 5 is set a century after the events of Diablo 4, in a Sanctuary where Diablo has already triumphed and its heroes have already been defeated: "Sanctuary has fallen. Diablo won".

A panel, hosted by Blizzard president Johanna Faries alongside the Diablo 5 development team, offered an early look at the game's world, classes, and creative direction. It confirmed two returning classes - Demon Hunter and Monk - alongside brand new class Plague Knight.

Beyond that, details were scarce, and we didn't get any insights into core gameplay systems, progression, or how any of this will actually translate into play.

Blizzard also confirmed that a Diablo animated series is in development with Netflix, though I'm afraid we didn't get many details about that, either.

"Sanctuary's darkness is spreading," the description teases. "Blizzard and Netflix are developing a new animated series set in the world of Diablo, bringing the franchise to a new screen. We'll have more to share as the series takes shape. Until then, stay awhile... and stay tuned."

The Diablo franchise has passed more than 130 million players worldwide since its original 1996 release, and this year marks its 30th anniversary.

For more, here's everything announced in the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony.

title: After Persona 3 Reload and Persona 4 Revival, remakes of the first two JRPGs are "something we'll probably eventually do," series producer says
author: Kaan Serin
content:
With Akechi song, I hope.

With Persona 3 Reload out the door and Persona 4 Revival next in line, series producer Kazuhisa Wada has said remakes of the first two games will "probably" happen as well.

Developer Atlus seems to be on a mission to revisit every high-schooling, demon-mashing, double-life-simulating game it's ever made. In 2024, the studio pulled the gun on Persona 3 Reload before starting work on Persona 4 Revival, coming next February. But Atlus may reach even further back for some new (old) source material.

In an interview with RPS, Wada said the team originally came up with the idea to remake Persona 3 and Persona 4 around the same time. The latter "had to be put" on the backburner for a while, but the intent for both was the same. "I think a remaster or remake is some kind of cultural preservation," he said, per a translator.

Wada continued to explain that it's Atlus' "duty" to make sure its older games aren't lost to time "and are still around in the modern day." With that in mind, "Persona 1 and 2 are something we'll probably eventually do, too." There you have it, folks.

Persona 1 and Persona 2 are also the only mainline games in the series that aren't readily available to buy on any modern system, making Wada's point about "cultural preservation" even more salient here.

Regardless, I think it always made sense to begin this remake voyage with Persona 3, the game that spawned the series' more recognisable features (social elements, dating, etc) and notably didn't include a major antagonist that might be tricky to depict in the same way nowadays (a rumour-fuelled Hitler reincarnation).

A few years back, a prominent Sega leaker claimed that Persona 1 and 2 remakes were in the works, alongside a Persona 4 remake that hadn't been made official at the time. It wasn't clear how substantially different those rumoured remakes would be, however.

title: Low poly horror Tumblebee combines the joy of tumbling bees with the not-joy of being chased by huge spiders
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Buzzkiller!

For the last few years I've been labouring to transform my terror of spiders into guarded appreciation, even wonder. I've been drawing pictures of spiders, and writing stories about them. When I spy a spyder (spider) in the wild, I make a strenuous display of hunkering down to utter words like "ooh, what a beautiful False Widow, such poetry of form". Then the spider moves a fraction, and I hoot and holler on out of there, pawing imaginary silk strands from my face. Videogames like Tumblebee are not helping with this endeavour.

I didn't even know Tumblebee had any terrible spiders in it, before watching the trailer. Nothing about the title implies being chased through earthen labyrinths by eight-legged fiends. It sounds like a jolly platformer, doesn't it? Or an apicultural take on Peggle. Here's the setup: the spiders have abducted your bee chums, cocooning them in a cave. You've got to rescue them before the spiders wake up and eat you.

From the looks of things, you aren't able to fly fast enough to escape the spiders, which is where the genre-resetting "tumbling bee" element comes in - you can roll, hop and bounce from mushrooms to put a few precious centimetres between yourself and those clutching forelimbs. The Steam page doesn't indicate whether you can get stuck in a web yourself, but that seems like a possibility. All of this plays out against a clangorous, roaring electronic score that makes the blood rush to my head.

Tumblebee launches tomorrow, 17th September 2026. I'm writing it up partly because it's from Agelvik, deviser of the excellent underwater hellshooter Death in Abyss, and partly because as noted above, I'm trying to exorcise my own arachnid demons. Spiders are marvels of nature, remember! Let's try to identify the ones in Tumblebee. Going by the size, I think that's some kind of Huntsman in the fourth screenshoarrgh get it off get it off get it off

title: Square Enix's two biggest 2027 games are being made by the same team, and its FF7 Revelation director just confirmed it
author: Vikki Blake
content:
"That’s really all on my watch now."

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi has confirmed that his own team, Creative Studio 1, is also the studio behind Kingdom Hearts 4.

Hamaguchi made the comments in an interview with Deadline, discussing Square Enix's plans for 2027.

Asked about the year ahead, Hamaguchi said the company sees Final Fantasy 7 Revelation and Kingdom Hearts 4 as the titles that will drive what he called a "big fight back" for Square Enix, quoting company president Takashi Kiryu.

"In terms of Square Enix and 2027, our President, Takashi Kiryu, says that next year is the big fight back for us, where everything turns around," Hamaguchi said.

"And obviously, between Final Fantasy 7 Revelation and Kingdom Hearts 4, those are massive titles that are going to push that. And both are being developed in my own studio, Creative Studio 1. So yeah, I’m really pumped up now for that. That’s really all on my watch now, so I’m going to be the guy who’s pushing all that forward."

That's not the same as Hamaguchi taking creative control of Kingdom Hearts 4, though. Nomura is still directing, with Tai Yasue serving as co-director. Hamaguchi's comment was about who runs the studio, not who's leading Sora's story.

As for Nomura, he recently addressed the newly announced Kingdom Hearts anime series directly for the first time, confirming that the series is officially in production and that he's been in close consultation with its scenario team and, where needed, its art team.

"I cannot say anything more at this moment, but the single piece of key art released serves as a hint," he said at the time. "Please let your imagination run wild as you await further updates."

If you're hoping to go into Kingdom Hearts 4 completely spoiler-free, now may be a good time to mute your socials. A massive information leak appears to have pushed full achievement lists for upcoming and unannounced PC games, including Persona 6 and Kingdom Hearts 4, online.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is due out on 8th April 2027, wrapping up the remake trilogy, while Kingdom Hearts 4 is currently pencilled in for the second half of the year.

title: The Witcher 3's story director says an ideal quest is 'constructed in such a way that the player puts the controller away, stands up, and starts walking'
author: @pcgamer
content:
The Witcher 3, being one of the best RPGs of its era, naturally has a lot of very good quests—quests with weighty, significant choices that give you pause to think. In speaking with PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens, story director Marcin Blacha says that pause is a sign that he and his team have done something right in a story choice.

"First of all, the choice has to make you think," Blacha says, "So it cannot be obvious. You cannot simply go after one of the choices by simply pressing A all the time, so that's the first thing. Second of all, in addition to having this balance, it needs to have its own gravitas. It must be serious. It must make you think about either life or humans or this particular problem or the difficulties that the characters may have right now.

"I always repeat that when you have a really big choice in The Witcher 3, it must be constructed in such a way that the player puts the controller away, stands up, and starts walking, thinking about the choice, and then goes back, and then the player picks one of the choices."

Which tracks—when I think back to the most impactful choices of the RPGs I've played, there's usually at least been a jarring, 'sit back and think' moment that's knocked me back into my chair, if not off it entirely:

"So it is about thinking," Blacha continues. "It is about making the player immersed into the game and the problems that characters have, but also saying something about either who we are or how the world works, or how difficult life can sometimes be."

In regards to the upcoming DLC, Songs of the Past, and whether it'll have any hard choices to make? "Obviously. I mean, we are not trying to avoid difficult choices, and we are not avoiding making players uncomfortable. So I can promise that you will have both in Songs of the Past, and sometimes you will regret [your choice] and you will need to load the game to repeat your choice."

title: Arc Raiders Expeditions may not come back: 'Maybe we'll scrap the whole system'
author: Andy Chalk
content:
Embark Studios announced a "pause" on Expeditions in Arc Raiders until early 2027 so it can rework the system to address longstanding issues and complaints that can't be handled with "incremental fixes." In a recent interview with PCGamesN, though, Arc Raiders executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said the studio might go even further by ditching Expeditions entirely.

Expeditions are essentially Arc's equivalent of prestiging in Call of Duty: High-level players invest time and resources into a "caravan" that ultimately—within the context of the game's fiction—enables their character to leave the Rust Belt forever. Practically speaking, it's a full reset of levels, skills, and inventory, in exchange for certain unique benefits conferred upon the player's new character. It's a major undertaking, and many Arc players haven't been happy with the amount of grind involved for a relatively minor payoff.

Announcing the pause in August, Embark said many of the issues raised by players, "like the tight departure windows, the reward structure, and accessibility for new players, need more than incremental fixes. They call for bigger changes." The fifth Expedition, set to depart at the end of September, will be the last until Embark has the overhaul finished—or just cans the whole thing, as the case may be.

"Was the system perfect? No, probably not," Grøndal told PCGN at Gamescom. "We want to make some significant changes to the Expedition system. But I think right now we're focused on, 'Yeah, they are what they are,' but the intent is to have them change.

"Maybe we'll scrap the whole system altogether. That is on the table, too. Right now, the team is trying to figure out what the next steps for Expeditions are."

When Embark will make its final decision on the fate of Expeditions remains, well, undecided, although nothing's going to happen until the Frozen Trails major update drops in October. But whatever happens, it seems clear that players should expect major changes.

title: Appendix to Barriers and Safeguards: Access to Assisted Dying for the Socioeconomically Vulnerable Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
A Comprehensive Descriptive Means

  • Volume 139
  • Issue 8
  • June 2026

Where jurisdictions have not yet clarified their stances as to particular safeguards, this Appendix characterizes their approaches as “Unclear.” If a jurisdiction imposes a waiting period but waives it in certain cases, this Appendix categorizes the jurisdiction as imposing the waiting period restriction. This is because exemptions are offered on a case-by-case basis,1 so default waiting periods are barriers to access in themselves because patients are unable to predict, at the time they choose to initiate the assisted dying process rather than to engage in self-help, whether they will be eligible. In the context of assisted dying, advance directives allow competent patients to issue written statements authorizing health care providers to provide or administer fatal medication at a later date, when they may have lost decisionmaking capacity.2

title: Federal judge blocks latest attempt to add Trump’s name to Kennedy Center
content:
News

Federal judge blocks latest attempt to add Trump’s name to Kennedy Center

Judge Christopher Cooper ruled on Tuesday that the Kennedy Center’s Board of Trustees cannot install memorials for President Donald J. Trump, or anyone else who is not former President John F. Kennedy, at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts without Congress’s approval.

This ruling followed a request from Joyce Beatty, an Ohio congresswoman and past member of the Board, who called on an emergency basis for the court to prohibit the Board from taking any steps on its most recent resolution.

On August 13, the Board passed a resolution to honor both President Trump’s present and future contributions in three different ways. The first is an inscription beneath the name of the Center that states “Renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump.” The second is an inscription to be added beneath the name once the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reaches $100 million, stating “Endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” The third is naming the previously unnamed physical grounds the Center sits on as “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” The Board had initially planned to enact this resolution by September 8, 2026, but later extended the deadline to October 8, 2026.

This resolution follows a court ruling four months earlier, on May 29, that had concluded the Kennedy Center had been named by Congress for John F. Kennedy alone, and that the federal law that created the Center prohibited any other name. That ruling had been used to strike down the Board’s earlier attempt to rename the institution in honor of President Trump. That order gave the board 14 days to strip Trump’s name from the building, website, and branding, and the center fully complied by removing the name from the building in mid-June.

The May ruling also restored voting rights to Representative Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio trustee who had brought the underlying suit after the board stripped her vote. The board’s latest resolution, which Judge Cooper blocked on Tuesday, is its second attempt in a matter of months to secure a place for Trump’s name at the Center.

After Judge Cooper’s ruling, the Board voted to close the Center on Tuesday, citing financial issues and the dispute over putting President Trump’s name on the Center. The Board had recently been floating multiple options for getting Trump’s name on the Center over fears that Trump would cease financial contributions if he did not receive the recognition he sought. The Center needs these contributions for much-needed renovations.

title: Hurricane Helene Washed His Wife Away From Their Mobile Home. Now New Residents Live on the Same Land.
author: Krista Stevens
content:
Dave Masters watched as his father’s house careened into a telephone pole and split in two, after Hurricane Frances lifted it from its foundation in 2004. Hayward County, in Western North Carolina, bought the house and declared the patch near the town of Clyde “permanent open space under a federally funded program to reduce the risk of future loss of life and property damage.” Not all homes were treated equally, though, in the aftermath of distaster. Hurricanes Frances, Ivan, and Helene, along with Tropical Storm Fred, all brought heavy rains and flooding to the nearby Hyder Mountain Road mobile home park. They’re “part the result of a gap in disaster policy that allows mobile home residents to be put in harm’s way again and again.” For The Assembly, in a piece produced for ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network, Ren Larson explains why.

The federal government’s programs to buy out disaster-prone buildings are “the cornerstone of the Nation’s system for emergency management,” according to the Federal Emergency Management Agency. But the program was developed with traditional homeowners in mind, and mobile homes, the country’s largest source of affordable housing, are often left out. Trailers, even when they become immovable and lifelong homes, aren’t typically considered real estate but instead personal property, like motorcycles and boats.

That still leaves people living on flood-prone land. For the state to actually buy that land, mobile home park owners have to take the buyout, and FEMA’s program offers little incentive for them to do so: They can’t collect from the government for lost rent or for the value of the mobile homes on top of the land. 

Some park owners say the payouts are not high enough to allow them to relocate; others aren’t even aware of the buyout program. So park owners regularly allow new trailers to move into the vacant spots. Art and Lynne Heinmiller, who own the Hyder Mountain Road mobile home park, did not respond to questions — which were emailed, texted and mailed via certified letter — about allowing trailers and campers to move back to where they’d washed away
